sense: more than the usual or the needed number

terms.gloss: besides, in addition: one more, two more
terms.grammar: adverb, beside the noun or the number
evidence: Verg. A. 11.285: sī duo praetereā tālīs …, glossed “two more” by Lewis & Short
Caes. B.G. 4.22: quicquid praetereā nāvium habēbat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin has no adjective for “extra”: it names the thing and adds praetereā, “besides”, or puts amplius with a number (see further). The same adverb opens an added point, “moreover”.

terms.gloss: an extra, an addition; something added on
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.138: hanc Scaurus dēmōlītus accessiōnem adjūnxit aedibus, Scaurus pulled the house down and built on an extension
Cic. Lael. 11: quid igitur hunc paucōrum annōrum accessiō juvāre potuisset?
terms.comment: The noun for the thing added to something larger: an extension to a house, a few extra years, a thing thrown in. Its first sense is an approach, a coming near; in medicine it is the onset of a fever (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: spare, extra: more than is needed
evidence: Cato Agr. 12: vāsa supervacānea, glossed “supernumerary, extra” by Lewis & Short
Cic. N.D. 2.121: ut nihil eōrum supervacāneum sit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its usual sense is needless, superfluous (Cicero, Sallust, Livy), so it suits a spare thing kept beyond what is needed, and can sound like a reproach: “one too many”.

phrases.latin: sī duo praetereā tālīs Īdaea tulisset terra virōs …
phrases.english: if the land of Ida had borne two more such men …

phrases.latin: Cape lōdīcem praetereā ūnam, sī algēs.
phrases.english: Take an extra blanket if you’re cold.

sources: Lewis & Short: praeterea · Lewis & Short: accessio · Lewis & Short: supervacaneus
